'''Michael Julius Alexander Moravcsik''' ({{IPA|hu|moravt͡ʃik}}; {{langx|hu|Moravcsik Mihály|italic=no}}; 25 June 1928 – 25 April 1989) was a [[Hungarian people|Hungarian]]-born [[United States|American]] theoretical high energy [[physicist]] whose areas of research included the two [[nucleon]] system, particle spin symmetries. He also made important contributions to the practice and study of science policy in developing nations, scientific methodology, and [[scientometrics]] (the science of science), especially the study of citation and citation indices.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01091696|doi=10.1007/BF01091696|title=Michael J. Moravcsik: A biographical sketch|year=1990|last1=Goldstein|first1=G. R.|journal=Few-Body Systems|volume=9|issue=2–3|pages=41–56|bibcode=1990FBS.....9...41G|s2cid=121390415|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Family and personal life==

Moravcsik was born June 25, 1928, in [[Budapest]].<ref name="auto"/> His father, [[Gyula Moravcsik]], was a professor of Greek philology and Byzantine history. His mother, Edit Moravcsik (née Fleissig), assisted her husband and taught language in Budapest. His grandfather, Fleissig Sándor, was a prominent Hungarian banker and politician. His brother was [[Julius Moravcsik]], an academic philosopher who taught at Stanford University. His sister is [[Edith A. Moravcsik]], a noted academic linguist who teaches at the [[University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee]]. He was married to Francesca Moravcsik and had two children, [[Andrew Moravcsik]], Professor of Politics and Public Affairs at Princeton University. His daughter Julia is a cognitive psychologist residing in [[Boulder, Colorado|Boulder]], Colorado.<ref name="auto1"/>

==Education, scientific interests and professional accomplishments==

Moravcsik began his studies at the [[Eötvös Loránd University|University of Budapest]], but left Hungary for the United States at the age of 20, accompanied by his brother Julius. He completed his BS in physics at [[Harvard University]] in 1951 and received his PhD from [[Cornell University]] in 1956.<ref>{{Cite journal|doi = 10.1063/1.2810505|title = Michael J. Moravcsik|year = 1990|last1 = Goldstein|first1 = Gary R.|journal = Physics Today|volume = 43|issue = 3|pages = 96–97|bibcode = 1990PhT....43c..96G|doi-access = free}}</ref> He was a research associate at the [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]] from 1956 to 1958. He was head of the elementary particle and nuclear theory group, theoretical division, [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] from 1958 to 1967. From 1967 until his death, he was a professor of physics at the [[University of Oregon]], at the Institute of Theoretical Science, where he was director from 1969 to 1972.<ref name="auto1">{{cite web | url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/226229660 | title=Michael J. Moravcsik: A biographical sketch }}</ref> At the time he was a professor of physics at the [[University of Oregon]].<ref name="auto">{{Cite journal|url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2FBF02018140|doi = 10.1007/BF02018140|title = Michael J. Moravcsik: Multidimensional scholar and hero of third world science|year = 1991|last1 = Garfield|first1 = E.|last2 = Small|first2 = H.|journal = Scientometrics|volume = 20|pages = 19–23|s2cid = 11912306|url-access = subscription}}</ref>

Two journals had memorial issues for Moravcsik: Scientometrics (Volume20, No 1, 1991)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://link.springer.com/journal/11192/volumes-and-issues/20-1|title = Scientometrics &#124; Volume 20, issue 1}}</ref> and Few Body Systems (Volume 9, No 2-3, 1990) <ref>{{Cite web|url=https://link.springer.com/journal/601/volumes-and-issues/9-2|title = Few-Body Systems &#124; Volume 9, issue 2}}</ref>

==Scientific interests and accomplishments==

Moravcsik worked on the nucleon-nucleon interaction in scattering experiments, and the pion-nucleon coupling constant.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.116.226|doi = 10.1103/PhysRev.116.226|title = Determination of the Pion-Nucleon Coupling Constant from n−p ''Scattering'' Angular Distribution|year = 1959|last1 = Cziffra|first1 = Peter|last2 = Moravcsik|first2 = Michael J.|journal = Physical Review|volume = 116|issue = 1|pages = 226–230|bibcode = 1959PhRv..116..226C|url-access = subscription}}</ref>

He also focused on science policy and its effects in developing countries. He was a science policy advisor to the [[Ford Foundation]], [[UNESCO]], the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], and the [[National Science Foundation]]. In addition, he made important contributions to the field of [[scientometrics]].<ref name="auto1"/>

In his spare time, Moravcsik wrote music reviews and was an amateur opera singer.

== Death ==
He died of an embolism on April 25, 1989, in [[Turin]], Italy, where he was collaborating with a colleague.<ref name="auto" /> He has three (posthumous) grandchildren: Michael Edward Hoke Moravcsik, Alexander deGogorza Moravcsik, and Sean Timothy Bowling.

== Books authored ==
* "On the Road to Worldwide Science: Contributions to Science Development" World Scientific, 1988.
* "Musical sound: an introduction to the physics of music" Springer Science & Business Media, 1987.
* "How to Grow Science" New York, NY : Universe Books, 1980.
* "The Two-Nucleon Interaction"

* "Optimally simple connection between the reaction matrix and the observables" GR Goldstein, MJ Moravcsik. Annals of Physics, 1976
* "Some results on the function and quality of citations." Moravcsik, Michael J., and Poovanalingam Murugesan. Social studies of science 5.1 (1975): 86-92
* "Measures of scientific growth" MJ Moravcsik. Research Policy, 1973
* "Nucleon-nucleon scattering experiments and their phenomenological analysis" Malcolm H. Mac Gregor, M.J. Moravcsik, H.P. Stapp (Dec, 1960) Ann.Rev.Nucl.Part.Sci. 10 (1960) 291-352
* "Analytic forms of the deuteron wave function" MJ Moravcsik. Nuclear Phys., 1958
